title: Capacity contract framing guide for architects
summary: A concise, technical-facing briefing and negotiation cribsheet for platform architects and procurement teams. Focused on how to frame guarantees for dedicated capacity: measurable SLAs, tenant isolation expectations, predictable throughput metrics, and practical contract language to accelerate procurement cycles.
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a short, pragmatic guide for platform architects and procurement partners who need negotiating language and decision criteria when buying dedicated inference capacity. It translates product-level capabilities (isolation modes, throughput controls, fallbacks) into procurement-ready commitments and tradeoffs that technical buyers care about.

Audience:
- Primary: Platform architects, infra leads, cloud procurement engineers.
- Secondary: Legal procurement, SRE, solutions engineers running vendor evaluations.

Topline positioning (one-liner for technical buyers):
- Predictable throughput with operator-grade isolation — dedicated GPUs and configurable routing guarantees so your production LLM calls behave like any other critical service.

Buyer pain we solve:
- Non-deterministic request latency during peak: bursts and noisy neighbors ruin user SLAs.
- Lack of contractual throughput guarantees from cloud-managed LLM endpoints.
- Risk that model upgrades or infra changes cause regressions in p99 latency and tail latency.
- Regulatory needs for data isolation and auditability that self-hosting is supposed to solve but is expensive to operate.

Key measurable guarantees to push for (how to ask for them):
1) Throughput commits: explicit milli- or token-based throughput units per second (e.g., 250k tokens/min sustained, burst to 350k tokens/min for 5 minutes). Ask for metrics exposure and billing tolerance windows.
2) Latency SLOs by profile: define SLOs for typical payload sizes and common model families (p50/p95/p99 for 128/512/2048 token requests). Avoid vague "low latency" language.
3) Isolation bandwidth: promised isolation levels (physical GPU isolation vs. tenant-aware cgroups) and quantifiable noisy-neighbor protection (e.g., <5% variance on baseline latency under 80% util).
4) Availability/uptime: inference-plane uptime for dedicated pools (e.g., 99.95% monthly availability) with clear measurement method and acceptable maintenance windows.
5) Degradation policies: graceful fallback behavior and automated model routing policies documented in contract — define how traffic shifts to compatible variants, expected latency delta when fallback occurs.
6) Error budget & remediation: SLA credits tied to measurable drops in throughput or availability and an agreed escalation path and runbook access.

Negotiation levers and tradeoffs (what the buyer can trade for cheaper terms):
- Longer committed term (12/24/36 months) for lower per-token price or higher sustained throughput.
- Relaxed burst/peak guarantees in exchange for guaranteed sustained baseline throughput.
- Accepting multi-tenant dedicated pools (soft isolation) vs. single-tenant hardware for cost efficiency — quantify expected isolation variance.
- Define allowed model families and quantization options (restricting model variants reduces kernel maintenance surface and helps price).

Suggested procurement checklist (technical + commercial items):
- Measurement and monitoring: access to raw telemetry (per-route latency, token counts, queue length), retention window, and a dashboard or API for pulling metrics.
- Audit & security: KMS integration details, audit log retention, and network topology (VPC peering, private links).
- Model version pins: ability to pin model versions and require notification of model changes or performance-impacting upgrades.
- Rollout controls: canary and gradual rollouts; automatic rollback clauses tied to defined regression thresholds.
- Capacity elasticity: autoscaling windows, billing for burst vs. reserved capacity, and pre-warm procedures for predictable batch spikes.

Sample contract language snippets (plain language for SOW/SA):
- Throughput Commitment: "Vendor will provide dedicated inference capacity to sustain at least X tokens per minute for the Customer's reserved pool with measurable telemetry reported every 1 minute. Burst windows to Y tokens/min are available up to N minutes per calendar day."
- Isolation Definition: "Dedicated pools shall be single-tenant at the GPU allocation level; noisy neighbor impact will not exceed 5% increase in p95 latency compared to baseline under 80% utilization."
- Latency SLO & Credits: "For requests with payload <= 512 tokens, Vendor will meet p99 latency <= 600ms for at least 99% of the billing period. Failures to meet this SLO will trigger SLA credits as defined in Appendix A."
- Change Control: "Model upgrades that materially change API contracts or token accounting must be communicated 30 days in advance and may be vetoed once per year by the Customer to permit validation runs."

Competitive notes (quick callbacks for procurement meetings):
- Hyperscalers (managed endpoints): strong global presence, but vague throughput contracts and noisy-neighbor risk on shared endpoints. Sellers often avoid granular p99 guarantees for inference workloads.
- Self-hosting (on-prem/GPU farm): greatest control but large ops cost, lacking vendor SLA and product features like automated routing and prefix caching tooling.
- Niche inference runtimes: good kernel/perf research but missing procurement/legal playbooks and enterprise-grade audit/KMS integrations.
- Redwood advantage (how to position internally and to buyers): unified offering that combines measurable throughput/latency SLAs, predictable pricing for reserved pools, and enterprise controls (KMS, VPC) — plus operations tooling (rollouts, model pinning) to minimize risk during upgrades.

Common buyer objections and canned responses:
- "We can do this ourselves cheaper." -> "You can, but our cost model includes software, ops, and regression protection: total cost of ownership for inference at scale is often higher when you account for SRE time and model maintenance. We offer measurable guarantees you can write into the contract."
- "What happens if models regress after an upgrade?" -> "We enforce model pinning and require staged rollouts with telemetry gates. Contract language can include veto and rollback rights for a limited number of upgrades per year."
- "How do we trust the telemetry?" -> "Provide API access to raw metrics, independent verification windows, and log snapshots for a sample period during ramp. We can include audit clauses and 3rd-party measurement tests in the SOW."

Open questions to resolve with product/legal before procurement pilots:
- Define exact telemetry schema and retention policy we will share with customers.
- Agree on a standard latency SLO matrix for the first wave of sales (e.g., 128/512/2048 token buckets).
- Standard sample contract credit calculations for throughput vs. availability breaches.
- Template language for allowed fallback models and acceptable latency deltas after failover.

Next steps (practical):
- GTM to finalize a short matrix of measurable SLOs for sales enablement (Diego).
- Legal to review and provide a small set of red-lineable SLA clauses for initial pilots (Priya).
- Solutions/AE playbook: create a one-page cheat sheet for buyer meetings with the three negotiation levers and example tradeoffs.

Notes to self / meeting fragments (working):
- Keep examples in contract in tokens/min rather than requests/sec — aligns better with burst accounting.
- Emphasize ability to pin model versions — this is a surprisingly strong ask from regulated buyers.
- For price modeling, show TCO example: self-host 2x infra + 0.5x ops vs. Redwood reserved pool + managed ops and integrated rollback tooling.

Document history:
- v0.1 initial outline 2025-11-03 (Maya)
- v0.2 added negotiation levers and sample clause drafts 2026-01-12 (Diego)
- v0.3 updated telemetry asks and open questions 2026-02-28 (Priya)

End of brief.  Use this as the living cribsheet when preparing procurement and architect-level conversations.
